practice.title: Offer What You Crave
agreedSteps: Take the things you crave, desire, or cling to — objects of the senses, praise, reputation, connection, time, money, specific people — and imagine offering them up to the Buddhas. It can be mental or physical. The point is to break down the barrier of self-grasping, miserliness, and craving that we put around ourselves.

While making offerings, hold three things in mind: (1) connect to the merit being created — remember that merit is the main cause of a Buddha's form body; (2) make the offerings as vast as possible — scale up from the room, to the city, to the earth, to the solar system, to the galaxy; (3) imagine and feel the bliss and delight the Buddhas are receiving — when we think about someone else's delight, we're actually feeling it in our own mind.
steps: For a specific craving like validation, start with step one: imagine you're in the presence of Buddha, and Buddha loves and accepts you perfectly as you are. Let that love be felt. Often the reason we want validation is because we don't feel loved — but Buddhas already love us completely.

Then ask: what can I offer that represents what I'm seeking? For something insubstantial like connection or self-worth, make it a 3D object — a beautiful trophy for praise, an interconnected tropical forest for connection. Offer it, and imagine the Buddhas delighted, receiving it with the mind of great bliss.

Support the practice with a fresh mind. When reading the Dharma or sitting down to offer, think: I'm a completely new person, doing this for the first time. I've never seen this before. I've never heard this teaching before. Ask the Buddhas to let you see it with the eyes of a beginner.

When a teaching feels boring or stale, don't take that at face value. Think instead: this means I do not understand this topic. Boredom is the signal of an old shortcut in the mind that isn't actually the meaning of the teaching. A fresh understanding of a teaching feels alive and vibrant, and we can't wait to hear it again.
practice.quote: When we give, when we make offerings, we're going over the line. We're breaking down the line of self and other, self and Buddhas, whatever. We're seeing no line. I'm not buying into this hallucinated boundary that my mind has made.

commentary.title: Making the Mind Fresh
content: Our mind operates through shortcuts. When we meet someone new, we experience them as new — we take in the details, ask questions, stay open. Within a month it gets simplified: I like them, I don't like them, they're this kind of person. Within a year it's a two-dimensional icon. That's them. All the nuance and difference disappears, even though they're actually changing in every moment. It's what the mind does to get by.

The trouble is when this habit leaks into the Dharma. Something we loved becomes two-dimensional and stale-seeming. It's not that the Dharma became boring — our mind became boring. The skill for clearing the stale gunk is simple: subtle impermanence. Think, I'm a completely new person doing this for the first time. I've never read this before. I've never heard this teaching before. Ask the Buddhas to let you see it with the eyes of a beginner. This is actually true — we are a completely new person in every single moment.

There are other hacks for the same mind. Imagine you're an alien showing up on Earth for the first time. You've never seen humans before, never seen Brooklyn, never seen a Buddha. You don't even know the texture of anything — is the carpet squishy or does it cut you? What does this food taste like? Or practice exchanging self with others: how does so-and-so see this teaching? How do the Buddhas see this? They see everything as new every moment. That's one of the qualities described in Ocean of Nectar.

commentary.title: Boredom Means You Don't Understand
content: When a teaching lands as "yeah, yeah, heard this, blah, blah, blah," the instantaneous thought we want to train in is: this means I do not understand this topic. All caps. Whenever there's boredom with a Dharma teaching, that means I don't understand it. Great — I'm hearing something I don't understand at all. This is a time for me to understand it.

The trick the mind is doing is slapping an old shortcut onto the teaching. "This means that" — which isn't really the meaning. And we're hearing our own shortcut, not what's actually being taught. That's what's boring. It's not that karma is boring or emptiness is boring — it's that the shortcut we chose to try to understand it is boring and overly simplistic. When we actually understand a teaching, we can't wait to hear it again. We're so happy someone is talking about it, because we have this living, vibrant experience of it getting watered by their words.
commentary.quote: If it's stale, it just means our mind is stale. And that just means we don't understand it.

commentary.title: Offering Is What Delights the Buddhas
content: Offering is defined as that which delights the Buddhas. That's it. So with all these descriptions of mountains of jewels and wish-granting trees and celestial palaces, the point isn't to constrain us to those specific images. The point is: use what's going to move your heart. Use what you find absolutely blissful and beautiful.

I talked to one of Geshe-la's most longtime students once, and I asked him what his Pure Land looked like. He said, a fresh mall. Like a shopping mall. He's just this older British guy who's lived at Manjushri Center for 50 years. So in his mind, the most blissful thing he can imagine is a fresh new shopping mall. It's a great teaching — what's blissful to us is completely dependent on our mind. Don't feel cordoned in by any of these traditional images.

A lot of us though are a bit dopamine fried. We've been absolutely fried with hits of dopamine from things human beings were never supposed to experience so many of. So what's beautiful and blissful has gotten miswired. The simple pleasures are blissful, but we might need to sit with them and rediscover their bliss. What's the bliss of a flower? What's the bliss of being offered a flower? The bliss of light? Of sound — like the peepers up at the temple this time of year, the most amazing, beautiful sound. If you sit in meditation and let these offerings come to the Buddhas, and imagine the bliss of their receiving, you start to see: these simple pleasures are just so beautiful.

commentary.title: Three Principles of Offering Practice
content: When we make offerings there are three things to work on in the mind. This isn't a rulesy thing — it's what's going to help us get the most out of it.

One: connect to the merit being created. Remember what merit actually is. There's a general sense — real good fortune, the potential to gain spiritual realizations. But there's a more technical meaning, which is that merit is the main cause of a Buddha's form body. So if we wonder why making offerings to Buddhas is meritorious, this is a big part of the answer. I'm making offerings to the form bodies of Buddhas. What does that do? It creates the cause to get a form body of a Buddha.

Two: make the offerings as vast as possible. One way I do it is to imagine the whole room filled with whatever I'm offering — beautiful lamps, lights, crystals. Then all of Brooklyn. Then all of New York, then the whole earth, then the whole solar system, then a whole galaxy — that swirling disk, all filled with light, all being offered. The point is just to try to make the mind as vast as possible. Break out of the little box mind we're in.

Three: imagine and feel the bliss and delight the Buddhas are having in receiving the offering. Here's the key: when we think about someone else's delight, we're actually feeling it in our own mind. Think about the joy of a family member who just got great news. If you're feeling their joy, that feeling is happening in your mind, not theirs. So whenever we make offerings, connect to the delight and bliss being experienced — and when we do, we feel it. These three things make the offering practice powerful and lovely. We just love doing it.

commentary.title: Miserliness, Not Pleasure, Is the Enemy
content: One of the main things that makes desire painful is not liking things — it's craving them. Feeling that we need them, that we don't want to part from them. That's what makes it so painful. If we could just think, that's nice, I'll take it or leave it — there's no pain. Oh, I met a nice friend. Oh, they don't like me anymore. Take it, leave it. Pick it up, drop it. No sunk cost fallacy in the mind.

The hard thing about dealing with attachment, unlike anger, is that there's a pleasure component. From one point of view anger is easier to work with, because anger is obviously painful — there's no pleasure anywhere. With attachment, there's a little bit of pleasure and a lot of pain, and that little bit of pleasure makes it much harder to deal with. Often we're willing to put in real effort for just that bit of pleasure.

So the practical work is to really try to see: what's the pain of miserliness? What's the pain of craving? Associate those words with pain. Once we meditate on this a little, anything we can do to overcome these minds starts to feel urgent — not urgent in a deluded, impatient way, but urgent in a driven, focused way. I don't want to keep this pain of miserliness. I don't want to keep this pain of craving anymore. I'm done with it.

commentary.title: Going Over the Line
content: Making offerings and practicing giving break down self-grasping, because the self-grasping mind imputes a little barrier around this lump of cells — around me. It's just an imputed barrier. There's no barrier. We're all cells in one body of life. We're one. It's just the self-grasping mind that hallucinates a boundary of an independent self. Every time we give, every time we make offerings, we're transgressing against that conception.

It's like the old nuclear proliferation protests where there would be a line, and if you crossed the line they'd arrest you, and people would just walk over to cross it. It was a transgressive act. Your line doesn't scare us. When we give, when we make offerings, we're going over the line. We're breaking down the line of self and other, self and Buddhas. I'm not buying into this hallucinated boundary my mind has made. We're eroding something.

Once we get the insight, we love giving things away because it tears at our miserliness. Especially our time — people in America are particularly attached to time, especially New Yorkers. Schedule, time, what's the time, you're late, you're late. But time is just a name, just imputed. So we start giving it away. It stings, if we're attached. And we think, this is great, I'm breaking down my miserliness. Same with the last slice of pizza when we know the other person really wants it and, technically, it's our slice. We say, you get that slice. It's like we're running onto Normandy. Charging into battle. We feel like such a heroic bodhisattva in that moment. Oh, that melted cheese and sauce. It's basically worth a dollar.

commentary.title: Recognizing Enlightened Beings
content: The text says that if we recognize the enlightened beings as having overcome all obstacles and possessing all good qualities, our practice of making offerings to them will bring us closer to their supreme attainment. Why? From one point of view, are we even recognizing enlightened beings if we're not recognizing that they've overcome all obstacles and possess all good qualities? That's not an enlightened being. That's, again, a simplification in our mind, a little 2D icon. We're not going to come closer to enlightenment in the same way relating to a 2D thing. It's still helping us, but not with the same power.

We have to work backwards. What's enlightenment, ultimately? It's thinking, basically, I'm a Buddha, not other than emptiness. I'm Heruka, Vajrayogini, not other than emptiness. That's the real truth. So we do generation stage and completion stage to directly help us see that. What helps us do those practices? Meditating on emptiness — and the practice of bodhichitta and exchanging self with others, so we learn to impute our I on a Buddha's body and mind and stop cherishing an ordinary self. What helps us do that? Renunciation, which makes us see it's just the nature of suffering to identify with an ordinary being. What helps us do that? Actually thinking enlightenment is possible at all. That's the Fourth Noble Truth — belief in true cessations, belief that liberation is possible.

So we can move all the way backwards through the stages of the path to basic refuge, to the simple thought: there are Buddhas, and I'm relating to the enlightened world. It's only when we start making a relationship with the enlightened world that we're going to want to develop renunciation, bodhichitta, emptiness, generation stage. Seeing Buddha images, starting to relate to them — this is making a relationship with the actual truth, with something beyond the ordinariness of life. First it seems separate from us, and then one day it seems like who we are.

commentary.title: Offering Specific Cravings
content: How do we apply this to worldly concerns — like wishing for validation, which is essentially attachment to reputation or praise? Step one is to imagine I'm in the presence of Buddha, and Buddha loves me and accepts me perfectly as I am. Just loves me so much. And I let that love be felt. That already helps a lot with the validation craving. Because often the reason we want validation is because we don't feel loved and valued — but there are already beings who know everything about us, and they love us completely.

Then, if we want to go further, we ask: what can I offer that represents the validation I'm seeking? Is it about connection? Self-worth? Actual words of praise? Whatever it is, imagine it as a 3D object we're offering away. Something insubstantial like validation becomes much more powerful when we make it a 3D object. Geshe-la explains this in Great Treasury of Merit: offering our spiritual realizations as a little island with beautiful treasures on it. If we're craving connection, maybe the object is an incredible tropical forest in the Philippines — all interconnected, symbiotic, the water feeding the tree feeding the creature, an embodiment of connection. If it's self-worth, maybe a beautiful trophy. Then imagine offering it, and imagine the Buddhas delighted, the mind of great bliss receiving it. You just ask, how is that going to help my craving? And it does, like clockwork.
